78.title: The child at the well
78.hook: Mencius: anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well feels alarm, and that is the seed of goodness (Mencius 2A.6)
78.howItsDone: Students of Confucian thought learn the child at the well as Mencius's case that human nature is good, and read it alongside Xunzi's opposite view.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Samaritan stopped on the Jericho road where others passed by. Your line was go and do likewise.

Are people basically good? Or basically selfish, and just good at hiding it? The news on a bad day will give you one answer. A stranger carrying your groceries will give you the other. A Chinese philosopher named Mencius answered with a picture you can see in an instant. It opens a week of many houses: China, India, the Sikh Gurus, the Gospels and the Buddha, one story from each, each kept by its own people.
screen: `ARE PEOPLE BASICALLY GOOD?` → `A PICTURE YOU SEE IN AN INSTANT.` → `A WEEK OF MANY HOUSES.`

segments.voice: Mencius was a teacher in the line of Confucius, and later tradition called him the second sage, honored next to Confucius himself. The book of his teachings is simply called the Mencius. Every person, he says, has a heart that can't bear to see others suffer. His proof: suppose someone suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well. Anyone would feel a jolt of alarm and distress. Then he rules out the other explanations one by one. It isn't to get in good with the child's parents. It isn't to win praise from neighbors and friends. It isn't because you'd dislike what people would say, or, as some read the line, the sound of the child crying. It's there before any of that. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say everyone runs and saves the child. The picture stops at the jolt, the first flash, before any decision. That flash, Mencius says, is a sprout. He names four: the heart of compassion, the heart of shame, the heart of courtesy, and the heart that knows right from wrong. Everyone has them, like having four limbs. But sprouts have to be grown, like a small fire catching or a spring starting to flow. Not every Confucian agreed. A later thinker named Xunzi argued the opposite: that goodness has to be trained into people from the outside. Chinese tradition kept both voices. In Mencius's telling, a flinch at someone else's pain isn't weakness, and it isn't for show. It's the seed.

segments.voice: Think back over the last day or two for a moment when something in you leaned toward someone else: a wince when a friend was hurt, a wish to help a stranger, a flash of care before you thought about it. Don't judge whether you acted on it; just notice it was there before any reasons arrived. That's one of Mencius's sprouts, so let your attention rest on it, like sun on a seedling.
Sprout. Mencius's name for the jolt of compassion anyone feels before any reason, the first sign of goodness inside us.
Your line: the seed is there. Like any sprout, it still needs growing. See you tomorrow.

79.title: The river passes
79.hook: Confucius stands by a river and says it flows on like this, day and night (Analects 9.16)
79.howItsDone: The line from the Analects is often quoted in Chinese when people speak of passing time, and readers take it as a lament, a call to steady effort, or both.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mencius's sprout: the jolt of care at a child near a well, there before any reason. Your line was the seed is there.

Have you ever stood on a bridge and watched the water go under? It's oddly hard to walk away from. The water you're looking at is gone before you've finished looking, and yet the river stays exactly where it is. Kids stare at it. Old people stare at it. Nobody has to explain why. In China, long ago, a teacher stood by a stream and said one short sentence. Readers still argue about what he meant.
screen: `WATCHING WATER FROM A BRIDGE.` → `GONE, AND STILL THERE.` → `ONE SENTENCE BY A RIVER.`

segments.voice: The teacher is Confucius, and the sentence is in the Analects, the collection of his sayings that, tradition says, his students gathered. In James Legge's old translation, it reads: "The Master standing by a stream, said, 'It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!'" That's the whole passage. No explanation, no moral. And because he didn't explain, readers hear two very different things in it. Some hear a sigh: time running away like water, day and night, and us getting older on the bank. Tradition remembers Confucius as a teacher who spent long years hoping a ruler would put his teaching to use; heard that way, it's gentle grief about time. Others hear encouragement. The river doesn't rest on its good days or quit on its bad ones. It keeps going, and over years it cuts through rock. Mencius, yesterday's teacher, praised water that comes from a real spring, because it flows on day and night and fills every hollow before moving on. Some later Confucian readers heard in the river the ceaseless working of the world itself. You don't have to choose; maybe both are true at once. Time does pass, and the way to meet passing time is to keep flowing with it, a little each day. In Greece, Plato reports the philosopher Heraclitus saying you can't step into the same river twice. Two thinkers, far apart, both watching water.

segments.voice: If you're near a river, a fountain, rain, or a tap you can run slowly, watch it; if not, pour a glass and watch the surface settle, or picture a stream you've known. Watch the water arrive and leave without trying to hold any of it. Notice your breath doing the same, in and out, never the same breath twice: just like this.
Confucius. His one sentence at the stream: it goes on like this, day and night. A sigh, or a push, or both.
Your line: day and night. The river keeps going, a little at a time. Day seventy-nine, done.

80.title: Satyakama tells the truth
80.hook: asked his family line, the boy tells the plain truth about his mother, and the teacher accepts him for it (Chandogya Upanishad 4.4)
80.howItsDone: Hindu teachers and readers of the Upanishads often tell the story of Satyakama Jabala as a lesson in truthfulness, and it is often discussed in debates about birth, caste and fitness to learn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Confucius at the stream, and water that keeps going. Your line was day and night.

Father's name. Previous address. Reason for leaving your last job. Forms ask questions like these, and there's often a small pull to round the answer off, to make it tidier than a life actually was. Now suppose the question is asked out loud, by a teacher a boy badly wants to study with, and the honest answer is: I don't know who my father is. That's where a boy named Satyakama found himself, in an old Indian text called the Chandogya Upanishad.
screen: `A FORM YOU'D RATHER NOT FILL.` → `THE TIDY ANSWER.` → `THE HONEST ONE.`

segments.voice: The Chandogya is one of the Upanishads, the philosophical texts that close the Vedas. Satyakama wants to become a student of the sacred teaching. In that world, a teacher would ask a new student his family line, his gotra. So Satyakama asks his mother, Jabala, and she tells him the truth. When I was young, she says, I moved around a great deal, working as a servant, and that's when I had you. I don't know your family line. My name is Jabala. Your name is Satyakama. Call yourself Satyakama Jabala. No cover story. The boy goes to the teacher, Haridrumata Gautama, who asks: what is your family line? Satyakama repeats his mother's words, exactly. And the teacher says, as the Upanishad tells it, that only a true Brahmin could speak like that. Go and fetch firewood, he says: I'll take you as my student, because you have not turned away from the truth. His name joins satya, truth, and kama, desire: one who loves truth. It suits him. People take the teacher's answer in different ways. Some hear a radical idea, that truthfulness, not birth, is what makes a person fit to learn. Others point out that the story still speaks inside the world of caste, and simply finds its highest mark in a boy's honesty. Either way, look at the heroes: a mother who didn't lie to her son, and a son who didn't lie for her.

segments.voice: Think of one place where you usually round things off: I'm fine, when you're not, a small exaggeration, a detail you always leave out. Nothing big; just picture saying the plain version once, kindly, to someone safe, and notice that you're still here. The text doesn't say whether Satyakama was afraid; it says he spoke.

Your line: the truth is enough. A plain answer, kindly given, was what opened the door. That's day eighty.

81.title: Honest bread
81.hook: Guru Nanak squeezes a poor carpenter's bread and it drips milk, a rich man's bread and it drips blood (Janamsakhi tradition)
81.carry: bread that drips milk, not blood
81.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago to teach kirat karni, honest work, alongside sharing and remembering God; the langar, the free kitchen at gurdwaras, shares food with anyone who comes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyakama: no family line to give, so he gave the truth, and was taken in. Your line was the truth is enough.

Two invitations to dinner arrive on the same night. One is from the richest man in town: a big feast, the best food, everyone important there. The other is from a carpenter down a side street, and dinner is a plain, rough flatbread made from a coarse grain. The choice looks easy. The guest of honor chose the carpenter. He's Guru Nanak, the first Guru of the Sikhs, and the story is about what's inside a loaf of bread.
screen: `TWO DINNER INVITATIONS.` → `THE RICH MAN'S FEAST.` → `THE CARPENTER'S ROUGH BREAD.`

segments.voice: Guru Nanak lived in Punjab, and Sikhs honor him as the founder of their path. Many stories of his life are kept in the Janamsakhis, life stories told and written down by his followers. Sikhs treasure them as stories of the Guru, and they're separate from the scripture itself, the Guru Granth Sahib. On his travels, Guru Nanak comes to the town of Saidpur and stays with a poor carpenter named Bhai Lalo, eating the simple bread Lalo earns with his own hands. A wealthy official, Malik Bhago, is holding a great feast, and he's offended that the famous holy man is staying in a carpenter's hut. He demands that Nanak come, and asks why he refused his fine food. Nanak asks for two pieces of bread: one from Bhago's feast, one from Lalo's kitchen. He holds one in each hand and squeezes. From Lalo's bread, the story says, drips milk. From Bhago's, drips blood. Bread made by honest work, and bread made by squeezing the poor. Whatever you make of the miracle, the point is plain. In Sikh teaching, kirat karni, earning an honest living, goes together with vand chhakna, sharing what you have, and naam japna, remembering God. A line in the Guru Granth Sahib puts it simply: the one who earns by their own work and gives some away has found the path. And Lalo? His name appears in one of Guru Nanak's hymns in the scripture. The feast is only in the story. The carpenter is in the hymn.

segments.voice: If you have something to eat nearby, bread, fruit, a cup of tea, hold it; if not, think of your last meal. Think of the hands it passed through, someone who planted it, picked it, carried it, baked it, stocked the shelf, and then of your own hands and the work that paid for it. Take a slow bite or sip if you can, taste it properly, and let it be enough.
Honest bread. The carpenter's rough bread that, in the story, dripped milk in Guru Nanak's hand, because it was earned without harming anyone.
Your line: bread that drips milk, not blood. Honest work, and something left to share. See you tomorrow.

82.title: Feet toward the Kaaba
82.hook: resting at Mecca, Nanak is told to move his feet away from God's house, and asks where God is not (Janamsakhi tradition)
82.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the Mecca story from the Janamsakhis to teach that God is present everywhere; Muslims face the Kaaba in prayer as the direction that unites them, while teaching that God is not confined to any place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, honest bread: Lalo's rough loaf that dripped milk in Guru Nanak's hand. Your line was bread that drips milk, not blood.

There's usually a place where you lower your voice without being told. A church, a mosque, a temple, a grandmother's living room, a grave. Something in the body knows to be careful there. And you've probably seen someone get it wrong: shoes on where they should be off, a laugh at the wrong moment, feet up on the wrong chair. Today's story, from the Sikh tradition, starts with exactly that kind of moment: a tired traveler at the holiest place in Islam, lying down with his feet pointing the wrong way.
screen: `A PLACE YOU GO QUIET.` → `FEET ON THE WRONG CHAIR.` → `A TRAVELER AT MECCA.`

segments.voice: The Janamsakhis, the life stories of Guru Nanak from yesterday, say that on one of his long journeys he traveled west, as far as Mecca. Muslim histories don't record this visit, and historians debate whether it happened as told. But Sikhs have loved the story for centuries. Nanak arrives tired and lies down to sleep near the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine at the center of the Grand Mosque, which Muslims around the world face when they pray. His feet point toward it. A local religious official finds him, upset, and you can see why: to him it looks like deep disrespect. He tells Nanak to take his feet away from the house of God. And Nanak answers, as the story is told: then please turn my feet in a direction where God is not. In some versions, the official grabs his feet and drags them around, and wherever they point, the Kaaba seems to be there. In others, the words alone are enough. Either way, the official goes quiet. Here's what makes the story generous rather than a put-down: Muslims teach this too. The Kaaba is the direction of prayer, the house dedicated to God, not a place God is kept. The Qur'an says that to God belong the east and the west, and wherever you turn, there is the face of God. So the official and the Guru aren't really on opposite sides. Nanak just asked the question out loud, and it travels anywhere. If there's something sacred, where is it not? The kitchen floor. The bus. The ground under your feet right now.

segments.voice: Sit or stand with both feet flat, and notice the soles of your feet: the pressure, the temperature, the floor pushing back. Whatever this ground is, carpet, concrete, grass, it's holding you up without being asked. If you have a sense of the sacred, ask Nanak's question quietly, is it here too, and if you don't, simply notice being held.

Your line: where is it not. The question works in any room you are in. Day eighty-two.

83.title: The prodigal son
83.hook: a father runs down the road to a son who wasted everything (Luke 15:11–32)
83.howItsDone: Christians read the parable of the prodigal son as a picture of God's welcome to anyone who returns, and it is read often in churches, especially in seasons of repentance such as Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kaaba, and Guru Nanak's question at Mecca. Your line was where is it not.

There's a message people put off sending. The one to someone they let down, or drifted from, or said something to that they regret. It gets drafted in the head a dozen times. Hey, I know it's been a while. I know I messed up. The apology gets rehearsed until it's perfect, along with every way it could go wrong. Jesus told a story about a young man doing exactly that, rehearsing his apology the whole long walk home. And the great surprise is what happens before he gets to say it.
screen: `THE MESSAGE PUT OFF.` → `THE REHEARSED APOLOGY.` → `A LONG WALK HOME.`

segments.voice: It's in Luke, chapter fifteen, the third in a row of stories about lost things: a lost sheep, a lost coin, a lost son. A man has two sons. The younger asks for his share of the inheritance now, while his father is still alive. Some readers hear in that something close to: I wish you were dead. The father gives it. He goes to a far country and spends it all. Famine comes, and he ends up feeding pigs, so hungry he'd have eaten their food. Then, in the King James words, "when he came to himself." He will go home and say: I've sinned; I'm not worthy to be your son; take me on as a hired worker. He rehearses it. Here's the verse the story turns on: "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." Some readers take the far-off seeing to mean he'd been watching the road. Some commentators note that grown men of standing rarely ran in public. The son starts his speech, and never reaches the hired-worker part. Bring the best robe, a ring, shoes; kill the fattened calf. "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found." But the older son, out in the field, is furious the waster gets a party. And the father goes out to him too. The story never says if the older brother comes in. Christians read the father as a picture of God's welcome. The door is open for both sons.

84.title: The raft
84.hook: the Buddha: a raft is for crossing, not for carrying on your head afterward (Majjhima Nikaya 22)
84.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the simile of the raft to explain that the teachings are tools for liberation rather than possessions to cling to or argue over.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prodigal: a son who wasted everything, and a father who saw him far off and ran. Your line was he ran.

What do you do with a useful thing once it's done its job? Every path has its methods: ways of praying, sitting, learning. And this has been a week of many houses. Mencius and the child at the well. Confucius watching the river. Satyakama's plain truth. Guru Nanak's honest bread, and his feet toward the Kaaba. A father running down a road. Chinese, Hindu, Sikh and Christian stories, each from its own home. The week ends with the Buddha, and his answer to that odd question.

segments.voice: The Buddha is speaking to his monks, in the twenty-second discourse of the Middle Length collection. Suppose, he says, a man on a long journey comes to a wide river. The near bank is dangerous and frightening; the far bank is safe. No ferry, no bridge. So he gathers grass, sticks, branches and leaves, ties them into a raft, and paddling with his hands and feet, he makes it across. On the safe side, he thinks: this raft was so useful to me. I should pick it up and carry it on my head wherever I go. Would that man be doing the right thing with the raft? the Buddha asks. No, say the monks. He should pull it up on the shore, or leave it floating, and go on his way. Then the startling part: in the same way, the Buddha says, the teaching itself is like a raft. It's for crossing over, not for holding onto. He's talking about his own teaching. Buddhist teachers read that letting go in more than one way. It doesn't mean the teaching is useless; the whole story says how useful the raft was. It means don't cling to it, don't turn it into something to own and defend. Use it to cross. Ordinary life has rafts too: the training wheels, the flashcards, the alarm you needed for years and then didn't. There's no shame in how much you needed a raft. The only mistake is carrying it on your head after you've reached the shore.
screen: `A WIDE RIVER, NO BRIDGE.` · `GRASS, STICKS, HANDS AND FEET.` · `CARRY IT ON YOUR HEAD?` · `THE TEACHING IS FOR CROSSING.` · then, large: `LEAVE THE RAFT.`

segments.voice: Think of the habits, rules and tricks that get you through a day, and find one you still carry after it stopped helping: a way of working that fit an old job, a rule from a hard season that's over now. Thank it honestly; it got you across something. Then picture setting it down on the bank, gently, and walking on a few steps without it.
The raft. The Buddha's picture of a teaching as something for crossing over, useful, and then set down on the far shore.
Your line: leave the raft. Useful once doesn't mean carried around forever. Day eighty-four, done.
